clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive defect of ganglioside biosynthesis caused by biallelic ST3GAL5 variants encoding GM3 synthase (lactosylceramide alpha-2,3-sialyltransferase).
Presents in early infancy with intractable epilepsy, marked irritability and arrest then regression of development, progressing to profound intellectual disability.
A distinctive later feature is cutaneous dyspigmentation in a salt-and-pepper pattern of hyper- and hypopigmented macules, giving the eponymous salt-and-pepper syndrome.
Acquired sensorineural deafness and cortical visual impairment are common, and a movement disorder with choreoathetosis and dystonia develops.
First delineated in the Old Order Amish as the Amish infantile epilepsy syndrome, it is now recognised across several populations.

Because the block is in glycosphingolipid (ganglioside) synthesis rather than protein N-glycosylation, serum transferrin isoelectric focusing is usually normal, so a normal CDG screen does not exclude it.
Feeding difficulty with faltering growth and stagnant head circumference (acquired microcephaly) is typical.
reference.pathophysiology: ST3GAL5 encodes GM3 synthase, the sialyltransferase that transfers sialic acid onto lactosylceramide to form GM3, the obligate precursor of the a- and b-series complex gangliosides. Loss-of-function variants abolish GM3 synthesis and deplete the downstream gangliosides that are heavily enriched in neuronal and melanocyte membranes and that are essential for synaptic signalling, receptor modulation and cell-cell recognition, while precursor and alternative-series glycolipids accumulate. Profound deficiency of complex gangliosides in the developing brain produces the severe infantile epileptic encephalopathy and progressive neurodegeneration, and disturbed melanocyte glycolipids account for the characteristic salt-and-pepper dyspigmentation.
additionalDifferentials: ST3GAL3-related epileptic encephalopathy and intellectual disability (a related sialyltransferase defect)
B4GALNT1 deficiency (hereditary spastic paraplegia SPG26, with overlapping ganglioside-series disturbance)
Other early-infantile epileptic encephalopathies (CDKL5, STXBP1, KCNQ2)
GM1 and GM2 gangliosidoses and neuronal ceroid lipofuscinoses (progressive neuroregression with seizures)
Menkes disease and other neurodegenerative disorders with pigmentary or hair changes
Peroxisomal and mitochondrial encephalopathies of infancy
additionalInvestigations: Molecular testing of ST3GAL5 with an epileptic-encephalopathy or CDG gene panel, or exome sequencing
Plasma glycosphingolipid and ganglioside profiling (reduced GM3 and downstream species)
EEG (often multifocal epileptiform activity or hypsarrhythmia-like patterns)
Serum transferrin isoelectric focusing (typically normal, helping to exclude N-glycosylation CDGs)
Ophthalmology and audiology assessment, including visual evoked potentials and brainstem auditory responses
redFlags: Onset of refractory seizures with developmental arrest in early infancy
Progressive loss of vision and hearing
Feeding failure with aspiration risk and faltering growth
reference.prognosis: The disorder is severe and progressive, producing profound and permanent neurodisability; many affected children have a markedly shortened lifespan, and care is supportive with a focus on seizure control, feeding and comfort.
pitfalls: Relying on a normal transferrin CDG screen to exclude the diagnosis, as ganglioside defects are not detected by that test.
Attributing the picture to a channelopathy epileptic encephalopathy and stopping the genetic work-up before ST3GAL5 is tested.
Overlooking the diagnostic value of the salt-and-pepper dyspigmentation, which may appear only later in the course.
Misreading acquired microcephaly and regression as a static encephalopathy.
references: Physician's Guide to the Diagnosis, Treatment and Follow-up of Inherited Metabolic Diseases
Congenital disorders of glycosylation and glycosphingolipid biosynthesis reviews
Paediatric neurology and neurometabolic reference texts
management: No disease-specific therapy exists; care is supportive with a focus on seizure control, feeding and comfort
Antiseizure medications for the intractable infantile epilepsy
Nutritional support and management of feeding difficulties, including gastrostomy where needed
Management of the movement disorder with choreoathetosis and dystonia, and of marked irritability
Audiology support for acquired sensorineural deafness and ophthalmology/visual support for cortical visual impairment
Multidisciplinary developmental, physiotherapy and palliative care given the progressive neurodegeneration
Genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive disorder, with family screening, noting the founder variant in the Old Order Amish
